name: Elena Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and what you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a trainee on a surface miner at a big bauxite mine, that's the ore they make aluminium from. A surface miner is like a giant road-cutting machine, it has a drum with teeth that shaves the ore layer off flat so the trucks can load it. I've been on it about a year, before that I was on the water cart, spraying the roads so the dust stays down. Twelve-hour days, a lot of watching the depth readings and listening for the drum.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's precise. You're cutting to a few centimetres and the grade control people tell you if you got it right, it's like a test every day. Hard part is I'm still slow on the turns and my supervisor, Hendrik, is very patient in a way that makes me feel worse. And money: my husband Rafael started a coffee van last year, and every cent we had went into the loan for it, so right now we're living on my trainee pay and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read five pictures of the future and ask the same questions for each. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, just not magic. I use AI every day for the coffee van's books and orders, so I'd be the one saying 'it's a good tool, people, calm down.' Probably post that in the small-business group I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, that's a good picture. The mine keeps going, I get better on the surface miner, and Rafael's van gets a couple of years to grow. The AI I use stays cheap and helpful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, get signed off on the surface miner on my own by mid-year. Use AI to sort out the van's stock and roster, maybe get it to find a second spot for Rafael near the hospital. Start paying the van loan down faster once it turns a profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty happy, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How exactly do you use AI for the van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every night I put in what sold and it tells me what to order, how much milk, how many pastries. It also writes the posts for the van's page, and I fix them so they sound like Rafael and not a robot. It's saved us maybe two hours a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone at the mine know you do all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hendrik does, I showed him. He asked if it could do his tax. I told him I'd help him for a coffee voucher. That's how business works in a small town.

S0.say: I'd say AI is useful but not magic, and that people should calm down because it's a good tool. I'd post that in the small-business group I'm in.
S0.think: I think it's a good picture for me: the mine keeps going, I improve on the surface miner and my husband's coffee van gets time to grow. The AI I use stays cheap and helpful.
S0.do: Keeps working and aims to be signed off on the surface miner by mid-year. Uses AI to manage the coffee van's stock and roster, looks for a second site near the hospital, and pays the van loan down faster once it's profitable.
S0.quote: I told him I'd help him for a coffee voucher. That's how business works in a small town.
S0.fieldNote: She's a natural small-business person who already runs her husband's coffee van with AI tools every night. A quiet AI world suits her because it keeps both incomes on track. Her humour is dry and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how progress works, some jobs go and new ones come, and the people who learn fast will be fine. I'd also say families and churches need to look after the ones who struggle, not just wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a surface miner is very automatable. It's already GPS guided, you're mostly watching numbers. So my seat probably goes. But I'm the person on my crew who's best with the screens, so I'd try to be the one watching four machines instead of driving one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Hendrik and the training office the first week and say put me on whatever automation trial you've got. At night I'd learn the remote systems with AI explaining the manuals. And I'd push Rafael's van harder, maybe add a second van in a year, because two incomes are safer than one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited, a bit nervous about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A second van with no savings sounds risky. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully. I'd wait until the first loan is half paid, then talk to the bank with real numbers, which I'd have, because I track everything. If the bank says no, we wait. I'm happy with risk but not with stupid risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older guys on the water carts. Water carts will be the first to drive themselves, it's a road and a spray. A couple of them don't even have email. I'd offer to help them, but some are too proud to ask a young woman for help.

S1.say: I'd say this is how progress works, some jobs go and new ones come, and fast learners will be fine. I'd also say families and churches should look after those who struggle rather than waiting for government.
S1.think: I think a surface miner is very automatable and my seat probably goes. But I'm the best with screens on my crew, so I'd aim to be the one watching four machines instead of driving one.
S1.do: Volunteers for any automation trial in the first week and learns the remote systems at night with AI explaining the manuals. Grows the coffee van and plans a second van in a year, but only once the first loan is half paid.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and excited, a little nervous about money.
S1.quote: I'd try to be the one watching four machines instead of driving one.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady disruption as an opening and plans to move first. Her traditional outlook shows in wanting families and churches to care for those left behind. She draws a clear line between taking risks and taking stupid ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock and people need to pull together, families, churches, businesses. I wouldn't say the government should run everything, but I'd say they shouldn't make it harder with red tape either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years worries me, even though I like change. If AI can do any job, it can also run a coffee van, order stock and maybe make the coffee with a robot arm. So both our incomes are exposed at the same time, and we still owe on the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years hard. Take every overtime shift, pay down the van loan as fast as possible so we own it outright. I'd look for the people building or installing the robots in our region and get a job with them early. And I'd think about using the AI ourselves, a robot coffee machine in the van, so we're the ones automating, not the ones being automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be making plans at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A robot coffee machine would put Rafael out of a job too, wouldn't it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if he owns it. That's the difference. If we own the machine, he's the owner, not the worker. He'd hate it at first, he loves talking to the nurses at six in the morning. But owning is safer than being owned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your mine pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My phone plan, the streaming, the gym I don't go to. Then I'd ask my parents if we could move into their place for a while, they've got the room since my brothers left. Family first, before any office.

S2.say: I'd say it's a shock and families, churches and businesses need to pull together. I wouldn't want government running everything, but it shouldn't make things harder with red tape either.
S2.think: I think two years worries me because AI could run a coffee van too, so both our incomes are exposed at once while we still owe on the van. Even liking change doesn't fix that.
S2.do: Takes every overtime shift and pays down the van loan as fast as possible. Seeks a job with the companies installing robots in the region and looks at buying a robot coffee machine for the van so they own the automation.
S2.feel: Anxious, making plans at two in the morning.
S2.quote: If we own the machine, he's the owner, not the worker.
S2.fieldNote: Her answer to the fast picture is to own the automation rather than be replaced by it, which is a distinctive move for someone with no savings. She recognises both household incomes are exposed. Family, not government, is her fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so let's get on with it. Businesses that move first will survive. I'd want the government to fund apprenticeships and short courses, but mostly to get out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. Enough time to own the van outright and maybe the second one too, and to get into a remote operations job at the mine. I'd be thirty-two with a small business and some tech skills. That's not a bad spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one: van loan down by half, me in the remote operations trial. Year two: the second van, if the numbers say yes, and maybe a technical diploma at night. I'd also put away a little every month for the first time, because the van's taught me what happens when you have no buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a busy way, not a scared way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the van taught you about having no buffer. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In March the espresso machine broke and the repair was more than our rent. We had to put it on a credit card and we're still paying it. Ever since, I check the machine every week like it's a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd try to own the machines. Does that still hold with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even more. With five years I'd have time to see which machines are worth buying. I'd rather buy the second robot than the first, the first one always has problems.

S3.say: I'd say we've been warned, so let's get on with it, and the businesses that move first will survive. Government should fund apprenticeships and short courses but mostly get out of the way.
S3.think: I think five years is enough to own the van outright, maybe a second one, and get into remote operations at the mine. At thirty-two with a business and tech skills, that's not a bad spot.
S3.do: Halves the van loan and joins the remote operations trial in the first year, then adds a second van if the numbers work and starts a night technical diploma. Saves a little every month after a costly espresso machine breakdown.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but busy rather than scared.
S3.quote: I'd rather buy the second robot than the first, the first one always has problems.
S3.fieldNote: The broken espresso machine is a sharp detail that explains why she now wants a buffer. She's eager about technology but sensible about timing purchases. Five years makes her plan feel achievable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so stop worrying and start planning. Learn something, start something, look after your family. I'd say that at church and in the business group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd come out of it fine. Ten years is enough to build a small business properly and to move from the mine into something technical. And maybe have children, which Rafael and I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the five-year plan but calmer. I'd do the full two-year technical diploma, not a rushed course. Build the coffee business to two or three vans with good systems, a lot of it run with AI. And we'd probably start a family around year three, once the business is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're very confident. Is there anything that would knock you off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Health, or a bad year with the business. And if the town shrinks because the mine shrinks, there's no one to sell coffee to. That one keeps me honest. A coffee van in an empty town is just a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if the town did shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the mine, it's a business, it has to compete. People who didn't plan, partly. And a government that makes it hard to start a business here, all the permits I had to do for one van. If they made that easier, people would fill the gap themselves.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so stop worrying and start planning: learn something, start something and look after your family. I'd say it at church and in the business group.
S4.think: I think I'd come out of it fine, with time to build a small business properly, move into technical work and maybe have children. Ten years is enough.
S4.do: Completes a full two-year technical diploma and grows the coffee business to two or three vans run largely with AI systems. Plans to start a family with her husband around year three once the business is steady.
S4.quote: A coffee van in an empty town is just a van.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she's openly optimistic, but she named her real weak point: the business depends on the mining town surviving. She blames permits and red tape, not the mine. Family plans are part of her timeline rather than something she'd sacrifice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the mine pay and the coffee van could go at the same time, and we'd still owe the bank. What would help is cheap loans for small businesses in mining towns, less paperwork to start one, and short paid courses so people can switch quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who's going to buy coffee. Everyone talks about robots doing the work, nobody talks about who still has money to spend. If the miners are gone, so are my customers.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about robots doing the work, nobody talks about who still has money to spend.
portrait: Elena Diaz is a 27-year-old trainee surface miner operator at a large bauxite mine, married to Rafael, whose new coffee van took every cent they had. She's traditional in her values, believes in family, church and enterprise over government, and uses AI every day to run the van's orders and books. In most pictures she moves first, volunteering for automation trials and planning to own machines rather than be replaced by them. The two-year picture makes her anxious because both incomes and the van loan are exposed at once, while ten years leaves her hopeful enough to plan children.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because the mine pay and the coffee van could go at the same time while they still owe the bank.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans and less paperwork for small businesses in mining towns, plus short paid courses so people can switch quickly.
